suggestions.title: Fintech Interview Prep Plan
suggestions.reason: Centralized document to outline the full preparation workflow with sections for research, practice, and reflection

content.text: Fintech Interview Prep Plan
This document tracks all steps of interview preparation: company research, technical topics, behavioral questions, and self-assessment. Update as you progress.
1. Company Research
Review the company’s products, mission, recent news, and financials. Note key differentiators in the fintech space (e.g., payment processing, lending, blockchain).
2. Technical & Domain Knowledge
Study core fintech concepts: API integrations, fraud detection, KYC/AML, risk modeling, and regulatory compliance (e.g., GDPR, PSD2).
Understand how the company handles transaction security.
Review common fintech stack technologies (e.g., AWS, Kafka, PostgreSQL).
Practice explaining a real-world fintech use case (e.g., peer-to-peer lending).
3. Behavioral & Situational Questions
Prepare strong answers using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) for questions like 'Tell me about a time you solved a complex problem' or 'How do you handle failure?'
Example: 'In my previous role, I identified a latency issue in payment processing and reduced it by 40% through better caching.'
Example: 'I once failed to meet a deadline due to miscommunication. I improved cross-team coordination by introducing weekly syncs.'
4. Self-Assessment & Confidence Check
Rate your confidence in each area (1–5) and identify gaps before the interview. Review with a mentor or peer if possible.
Complete company research and summarize key points
Practice 3 technical questions aloud
Record a mock interview with a friend or mentor
Next Steps
Schedule a mock interview with a peer or use a tool like Interviewing.io to simulate real-time questions. Review feedback and refine answers.

groundingDetail.original:
# Project Brief: Migrate Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

## Goals  
- Centralize and streamline team knowledge sharing by migrating from the current wiki platform to PlexiiWrite.  
- Improve content accessibility, searchability, and real-time collaboration across all team members.  
- Reduce administrative overhead associated with managing outdated or fragmented documentation.  
- Ensure continuity of critical project knowledge during the transition without disrupting daily workflows.

## Scope  
- Migration of all existing wiki pages (including project plans, process documents, and FAQs) into PlexiiWrite.  
- Configuration of new workspace structure, permissions, and templates aligned with team workflows.  
- Training sessions for key stakeholders and content owners on using PlexiiWrite features.  
- Ongoing support and monitoring of content quality and user adoption post-migration.  
*Excluded: Third-party integrations not directly tied to documentation; legacy tools used solely for code versioning.*

## Timeline  
- **Week 1–2**: Audit current wiki content, finalize categorization, and define migration priorities.  
- **Week 3–4**: Set up PlexiiWrite environment, configure access controls, and establish content templates.  
- **Week 5**: Begin phased migration of high-impact pages; validate accuracy and formatting.  
- **Week 6**: Complete full migration; conduct user testing and feedback collection.  
- **Week 7**: Launch official go-live with support team on standby for first 48 hours.  

## Risks & Mitigation  
- **Data loss or formatting issues**: Mitigated through staged migration, version control, and pre-migration content validation.  
- **User resistance to change**: Addressed via targeted training, clear communication, and early involvement of content owners.  
- **Delayed adoption**: Counteracted by establishing a “wiki champion” program and regular progress updates.  
- **Technical downtime during migration**: Scheduled during low-activity periods with rollback plan in place.

[Project status to be reviewed bi-weekly by the Product and Operations leads]  
[Final review date: [launch date]]

# Onboarding Guide for New Support Agents – First Week

## Welcome and Orientation

Welcome to the support team! This guide is designed to help you successfully transition into your role during your first week. You’ll gain a solid understanding of our tools, processes, and escalation procedures to ensure consistent, effective customer service.

Your first week will include orientation sessions, hands-on training, and shadowing opportunities. The goal is to build confidence in using key systems and to familiarize yourself with our support philosophy: empathy, accuracy, and proactive problem-solving.

## Key Tools and Systems

You will be introduced to the following core tools used daily:

- **Zendesk** – Our primary ticketing and case management system. Learn how to create, update, and close tickets, assign cases, and use search filters.
- **CRM (Salesforce)** – Used to access customer profiles, order history, and account details. You’ll learn how to retrieve relevant information to provide personalized support.
- **Knowledge Base (Internal Wiki)** – A searchable repository of common solutions, FAQs, and troubleshooting steps. Use it to resolve standard issues without escalation.
- **Slack** – The main communication channel for team coordination. Channels include #general, #support-ops, #onboarding, and #escalations.
- **Google Workspace (Gmail & Calendar)** – For internal emails and scheduling meetings with team leads or engineers.

All tools will be accessed via your company login. Your manager will provide a detailed walkthrough during your first day and assign specific training modules.

## Daily Responsibilities

During the first week, you will:

- Attend morning stand-up meetings to review open cases and team priorities.
- Shadow an experienced agent to observe real-time interactions and case handling.
- Complete assigned onboarding tasks in the knowledge base and tool training portal.
- Practice responding to sample tickets under supervision.
- Submit a weekly reflection report summarizing what you’ve learned and any questions.

## Handling Escalations

Escalations are part of our support process and are handled with clear protocols to ensure timely resolution and customer satisfaction.

### When to Escalate
You should escalate when:
- A customer reports a technical issue that cannot be resolved using standard solutions.
- The issue requires input from engineering or product teams.
- A customer expresses frustration or emotional distress, and a deeper investigation is needed.
- You have insufficient information to resolve the case within standard timeframes.

### Escalation Process
1. **Identify the need** – Confirm that the issue falls outside your scope of knowledge or resolution capability.
2. **Document clearly** – Include full ticket details, customer context, steps taken, and any error messages.
3. **Use the escalation workflow in Zendesk** – Select “Escalate” from the ticket action menu.
4. **Assign to the appropriate team** – Escalations are routed to:
   - Engineering (for technical bugs)
   - Product (for feature-related issues)
   - Customer Success (for account or contract concerns)
5. **Notify your manager** – Within 15 minutes of escalation, inform your supervisor via Slack to ensure visibility and accountability.

### Escalation Response Time
- All escalations must be acknowledged within 10 minutes of being submitted.
- The receiving team has 2 hours to respond with a resolution plan or next steps.

## Support for New Agents

You are not expected to resolve every issue on your first day. Your primary focus is learning and growing. Here’s what’s available to support you:

- A dedicated onboarding mentor who will check in daily.
- Access to a weekly Q&A session with the support lead.
- A checklist of common escalation scenarios to review before your first independent case.
- Feedback loop after each case to improve performance.

## Next Steps After Week One

After completing your first week, you’ll:
- Receive a formal performance review.
- Be invited to join team meetings and contribute to knowledge sharing.
- Begin taking ownership of cases under supervision.

Your journey with us begins here — stay curious, ask questions, and keep delivering excellent support.

— Support Operations Team

# Weekly Product Review Meeting Notes

## Meeting Date  
[Insert Date]

## Attendees  
- [Name 1] – Product Manager  
- [Name 2] – Engineering Lead  
- [Name 3] – UX Designer  
- [Name 4] – Growth & Analytics  
- [Name 5] – Customer Success  

## Agenda Items & Discussion Summary  

### 1. Pricing Page  
- Reviewed recent user feedback from the beta test group indicating confusion around tier differences, especially between the Pro and Enterprise plans.  
- Identified key friction points: lack of clear value propositions and inconsistent visual hierarchy across plan cards.  
- Action item: UX team to create a revised pricing card layout with clearer benefit statements by [date].  
- Engineering to ensure all plan features are accurately reflected in the backend data layer by end of week.  
- Next review scheduled: [date]  

### 2. Onboarding Drop-Off  
- Analytics show a 30% drop-off rate at the third step of onboarding (feature setup).  
- User interviews suggest users feel overwhelmed by the number of optional steps and lack guidance during setup.  
- Proposed solution: introduce a guided walkthrough with optional step progression, allowing users to skip or return.  
- Design team to prototype two versions of the onboarding flow by [date].  
- Engineering to assess technical feasibility and integration timeline with user data tracking.  
- Next review scheduled: [date]  

### 3. Mobile Beta  
- Beta group of 500 users reported high satisfaction with core functionality but noted performance lag during multi-tasking scenarios.  
- Crash logs indicate issues in image upload and navigation when switching between tabs.

bullets: Clear bug reports help developers fix issues faster

slides.notes: Start by emphasizing that bug reports aren't just about finding errors—they're tools for collaboration. A clear, structured report helps everyone understand the problem and act on it quickly.

slides.title: The Core Elements of a Good Report
bullets: Describe what happens (steps to reproduce)
Explain what should happen instead
Include expected vs actual results
Specify environment: device, OS, browser, version
Add any relevant screenshots or logs
Mention if the issue is new or recurring
slides.notes: These elements form the foundation of a useful bug report. Focus on clarity and precision—avoid vague language like 'it doesn't work.' Always include context so the developer can replicate the issue.

slides.title: How to Reproduce the Issue
bullets: Start with a clear step-by-step sequence
Use numbered steps for readability
Ensure each step is actionable and specific
Include user actions, not assumptions
Note any timing or conditions (e.g., after login, on page load)
Verify that the steps are repeatable
slides.notes: Reproducibility is key. The more precise the steps, the easier it is for developers to verify and fix. Avoid general statements like 'sometimes'—be specific about when and how the issue occurs.

slides.title: Clarity and Tone
bullets: Stay objective and factual
Avoid emotional language or blame
Use simple, direct language
Keep it concise—get to the point quickly
Focus on facts, not opinions
Always verify your description with real-world testing
slides.notes: Tone matters. A calm, neutral tone builds trust and avoids defensiveness. Focus on what was observed, not what might have gone wrong. This helps developers feel supported, not accused.

slides.title: Best Practices Summary
bullets: Always include steps to reproduce
Clearly state expected vs actual behavior
Provide environment details
Add visual evidence when possible
Check if the issue is new or known
Submit reports promptly when you notice a problem
slides.notes: Summarize the key takeaways in a way that’s easy to remember. Encourage team members to adopt these habits consistently—small changes lead to big improvements over time.

slides.title: Next Steps & Ownership
bullets: Review and validate each report before submission
Assign clear ownership for follow-up actions
Use a shared template to standardize reporting
Encourage feedback on report quality after fixes
Regularly review bug reports to identify patterns
Update processes based on team input
slides.notes: End with a call to action. Make sure everyone knows they’re responsible for the quality of their reports and that feedback loops exist to improve the process over time.
